h1: Pouring a German wheat beer with the yeast swirl at the end
title: How to pour a German wheat beer | Craft Beer School
desc: Pour a German wheat beer the Bavarian way: rinse the tall glass, pour slowly, then swirl the yeast left in the bottle and add it on top.
teaser: That last swirl of the bottle is not a show. It is where much of a hefeweizen's flavour and its famous haze come from.
standfirst: A German hefeweizen is unfiltered, lively and full of yeast. Pour it like a lager and you get a glass of foam, clear beer and a bottle with the best part still stuck at the bottom.
sections: Why wheat beer needs its own pour

Hefeweizen means yeast wheat beer. It is brewed with at least half wheat malt in Bavaria and bottled unfiltered, so a layer of yeast settles at the bottom of every bottle. It is also highly carbonated, often 3.5 volumes of carbon dioxide or more against about 2.5 for a typical lager. Tip it straight into a glass and it foams over.

The classic pour solves both problems. You pour gently to control the foam, then rouse the yeast left in the bottle and add it at the end. You get a tall glass with a thick head and an even, cloudy body. The yeast also matters for flavour: the banana and clove notes that define the style come from the same yeast you are about to swirl.
Use the tall glass and rinse it

The traditional weizen glass is tall and narrow at the base, wider near the top, usually holding half a litre with room for the head. The shape gives the foam space to rise and the narrow base keeps the yeast in suspension. If you do not have one, any tall glass of 500 ml or more is better than a short tumbler.

Rinse the glass with cold water just before you pour and do not dry it. A wet glass lets the beer slide down without frothing. Make sure it is beer clean too. Any grease kills the head. A wheat beer without a head is a sad thing. Serve the beer at about 6 to 8 °C, a little warmer than a pale lager.

1. Open the bottle and hold the wet glass at about 45 degrees.
  2. Pour slowly down the inside of the glass. Keep the bottle close to the glass so the beer has little distance to fall.
  3. As the glass fills, tilt it gradually upright. The head will start to form near the top.
  4. Stop when about 10% of the beer, roughly two or three centimetres, is left in the bottle.
  5. Swirl the bottle firmly in a circle for a few seconds to lift the yeast off the bottom.
  6. Pour the yeasty remainder into the middle of the glass, through the head.

You should end with a hazy, even beer and a dense head of three or four fingers that sits just above the rim.

The yeast in the bottle adds haze, body and a soft, bready edge. It rounds off the beer and makes it feel fuller in the mouth. Some drinkers also find it brings the banana and clove forward, though most of that aroma is already in the beer. Our guide to tasting banana, clove and pepper in beer explains where those notes come from.

Try one glass with the yeast and one without, side by side. The clear one tastes sharper and thinner. The cloudy one tastes rounder and more like the brewer intended. That comparison teaches you more about the style than any description.

Not every wheat beer wants the yeast. Kristallweizen is filtered and should be clear, so pour it gently and leave nothing behind. Some drinkers prefer a hefeweizen without the sediment, which is fine. It is your glass.

Belgian witbier is a different style, spiced with coriander and orange peel, but it is also unfiltered. The same gentle pour works for it, with a softer swirl at the end. Bottle conditioned ales from British or Belgian brewers are another matter: some carry a firm layer of yeast meant to stay in the bottle, so check the label before you swirl those.

Wheat beers are best young. Their banana and clove aromas fade with age. Heat speeds that up. A bottle that sat in a hot shop or a car for a week can taste dull and slightly papery, however perfect the pour. Buy from a shop that keeps beer chilled and check the packaging date where there is one.

Store bottles upright in the fridge so the yeast settles at the bottom, not along the side. That makes the controlled pour easier and keeps the swirl for the end where it belongs.

Pouring from too high is the main one. The beer hits the bottom of the glass, foams up and you end up waiting for the head to settle while the beer warms. The second is a warm glass straight from a hot cupboard, which makes the beer foam harder. The third is forgetting the yeast altogether and leaving the bottle on the table with a cloudy centimetre still inside.

If the head rises too fast, pause, let it settle for a few seconds and carry on. A wheat beer pour takes a little patience, perhaps 30 to 40 seconds start to finish.

Buy two bottles of the same hefeweizen, chill them upright and pour one with the full method and one straight into a dry glass. Compare head, haze and taste. You will not go back. For more on pouring other styles, see our guide on how to pour beer.
faqs: Should you swirl the yeast in a hefeweizen?
Traditionally, yes. Leave about 10% in the bottle, swirl it to lift the yeast and pour it on top for a hazy, fuller beer.
What glass is used for wheat beer?
A tall weizen glass, narrow at the base and wider at the top, usually half a litre with space for a big head.
Why does wheat beer foam so much?
Hefeweizen is highly carbonated and rich in wheat proteins that build foam, so it needs a slow, tilted pour.
What temperature should wheat beer be served at?
About 6 to 8 °C, slightly warmer than a pale lager, so the banana and clove aromas can show.
